Definist fallacy.notes: Definitions can clarify usage, but they do not settle the underlying issue by fiat. Rewording a problem is not the same as answering it.
caseStudies: Culture-war debates often define words like 'freedom,' 'woman,' 'democracy,' or 'terrorism' in ways that quietly smuggle the desired conclusion into the starting point.
Moral and political disputes frequently collapse into dictionary wars where one side pretends that owning the label settles the argument.

Fallacy of necessity.definition: Occurs when a condition that is necessary given someone's current description is treated as if it were permanently or universally necessary in the real world
Fallacy of necessity.example: He is unemployed now, and being unemployed means not having a job, so he cannot possibly be employed next month.
Fallacy of necessity.notes: Some predicates are necessary only relative to a present state or definition. That necessity does not magically extend across time, possibility, or changed conditions.
caseStudies: People sometimes move from 'this rule currently defines the category' to 'therefore the category could never be revised or altered,' confusing present convention with fixed necessity.
In institutional debates, a temporary legal or procedural status is often spoken of as if it were an immutable fact about what can never happen.

Package-deal fallacy.definition: Occurs when traits that are often bundled together by stereotype, tradition, or habit are treated as if they must always come as a package
Package-deal fallacy.example: He is a gamer, so he must be antisocial and male.
Package-deal fallacy.notes: Some traits do cluster more often than chance would predict, but the cluster is not a logical necessity. A familiar package can make us overread what belongs together.
caseStudies: Campaign and media narratives often assume that working-class, rural, religious, or college-educated identities come with one full political bundle attached.
People frequently expect hobbies, musical taste, fashion, or ethnicity to drag a whole associated worldview behind them even when the individual breaks the pattern.

Perfect standard.definition: Occurs when a messy range of better and worse cases is collapsed into a rigid perfect-or-failed binary
Perfect standard.example: One factual slip means this journalist is a liar rather than merely mistaken on that point.
Perfect standard.notes: Many human traits and performances come in degrees. Treating any deviation from an ideal as proof of total failure destroys the resolution needed for fair judgment.
caseStudies: Debates about media bias, moral character, and institutional trust often assume that if a person or outlet is not perfectly objective, then it is simply propaganda.
Public discussion of peace, tolerance, and fairness often ignores large improvements because some imperfection remains somewhere.

Reification.definition: Occurs when an abstraction is spoken of as if it were a concrete agent or thing in a way that misleads rather than merely using harmless metaphor
Reification.example: The market decided to punish us because it was angry.
Reification.notes: Metaphor can be useful shorthand, but the fallacy appears when agency, intention, or moral responsibility is attributed to an abstraction as though it literally possessed a mind of its own.
caseStudies: People talk as if capitalism, democracy, the algorithm, or history itself wants, fears, rewards, or punishes, which can hide the actual network of human choices and incentives underneath.
AI discussions sometimes slide from 'the model produced this output' to 'the AI wants this outcome,' smuggling in a stronger picture of agency than the evidence supports.

Teleological fallacy.definition: Occurs when a purpose, goal, or final destination is attributed to something without adequate evidence that such an end point was built into it
Teleological fallacy.example: Evolution created human intelligence because nature was trying to produce minds like ours.
Teleological fallacy.notes: Some things really are designed for purposes, but purpose should not be assumed where it has not been shown. Processes can produce outcomes without aiming at them.
caseStudies: People often speak as if history is automatically bending toward justice, collapse, nationalism, or liberation, as though social change carried its own guaranteed destination.
In technology debates, AI progress is sometimes framed as if it were inherently marching toward a single destined endpoint such as AGI rather than following contingent technical and social paths.

Affirmative conclusion from a negative p.definition: Occurs when a syllogism tries to draw a positive conclusion even though one of the premises is negative in a way that cannot support that conclusion
Affirmative conclusion from a negative p.example: This source is not anonymous. Anonymous sources are unreliable. Therefore this source is reliable.
Affirmative conclusion from a negative p.notes: Ruling something out does not automatically place it into the positive category you want. 'Not bad' does not by itself mean 'good,' and 'not that' does not by itself mean 'this.'
caseStudies: Tribal arguments often move from 'we are not them' and 'they are bad' to 'therefore we are trustworthy,' even though the conclusion has not been earned.
Media and politics frequently treat the failure of one rival source as if it directly validated a different source that still needs its own support.

Affirming a disjunct.definition: Occurs when someone treats an ordinary 'or' as if it were exclusive and concludes that one option must be false because the other is true
Affirming a disjunct.example: This video is either edited or misleading. It is edited, so it cannot also be misleading.
Affirming a disjunct.notes: Some disjunctions are genuinely exclusive, but many are not. Two options can coexist unless the statement or context really rules that out.
caseStudies: Budget rhetoric often suggests that because one policy tool is on the table, another cannot also matter, as if tradeoffs always come in only one-at-a-time form.
Public debate regularly acts as though a claim must be either emotional or strategic, either true or persuasive, either mistaken or manipulative, when in reality both descriptions may apply.

Affirming the consequent.definition: Occurs when someone reasons from 'if A, then B' and then wrongly infers A merely because B is observed
Affirming the consequent.example: If a clip is AI-generated, it may show warped hands. This clip shows warped hands, so it must be AI-generated.
Affirming the consequent.notes: A consequence can have many causes. Observing the result does not tell you which sufficient condition produced it.
caseStudies: Political misinformation often treats one suspicious-looking detail as proof of a favored cause, even though many other explanations remain live.
Arguments about fraud, manipulation, and AI generation frequently jump from a telltale symptom to a confident diagnosis without ruling out alternatives.

Denying the antecedent.definition: Occurs when someone reasons from 'if A, then B' and then wrongly infers 'not B' merely because A is absent
Denying the antecedent.example: If a study is peer-reviewed, it is worth taking seriously. This report is not peer-reviewed, so it is worthless.
Denying the antecedent.notes: One route to a conclusion does not have to be the only route. The absence of one sufficient condition does not automatically remove every other possible basis.
caseStudies: Debates about expertise often assume that if a source lacks one credential or prestige marker, there can be no meaningful evidence at all in what it says.
In everyday arguments, people often assume that if the ideal cause is absent, the observed effect cannot still arise through another path.

Exclusive premises.definition: Occurs when two negative premises are used in a syllogism even though they fail to establish the positive link the conclusion requires
Exclusive premises.example: No journalists are judges. Some judges are not activists. Therefore some activists are not journalists.
Exclusive premises.notes: Two exclusions do not by themselves tell you how the remaining categories relate. Keeping groups apart is not the same as establishing a valid connection among them.
caseStudies: Identity arguments sometimes pile up statements about what two groups are not and then pretend that the missing positive relation has somehow been proved.
This form often hides inside rhetorical contrasts where speakers rely on the sound of elimination rather than a genuine logical bridge.

Existential fallacy.definition: Occurs when a conclusion assumes that something exists even though the premises never established that any such thing exists
Existential fallacy.example: Every unicorn in this forest is shy. Therefore at least one unicorn in this forest is shy.
Existential fallacy.notes: Universal statements can be true even when the class is empty. Talking about all members of a category does not guarantee that there are any members to begin with.
caseStudies: Arguments about 'the average user,' 'the typical elite,' or 'the real moderate voter' sometimes slip from a hypothetical category into the assumption that a concrete instance must exist.
Formal and theological debates alike often move too quickly from what would be true if something existed to the claim that it therefore does exist.

Four terms fallacy.definition: Occurs when a syllogism seems to use three terms but actually uses four because one term shifts meaning halfway through the argument
Four terms fallacy.example: Nothing is better than open debate. A sandwich is better than nothing. Therefore a sandwich is better than open debate.
Four terms fallacy.notes: The surface wording can make the argument sound tidy, but the hidden term shift breaks the structure. A reused word is not enough; it has to keep the same meaning.
caseStudies: Public arguments often slide between technical and ordinary meanings of words like 'theory,' 'freedom,' 'bias,' or 'intelligence,' then pretend the resulting syllogism is valid.
Because the same label can carry prestige in one context and a thinner meaning in another, term shifts often smuggle in conclusions the premises did not support.

Illicit major.definition: Occurs when a syllogism distributes the major term in the conclusion even though the major premise never distributed it there
Illicit major.example: All billionaires are famous. No teachers are billionaires. Therefore no teachers are famous.
Illicit major.notes: Excluding one group from a subset does not exclude it from the wider property attached to that subset. The conclusion reaches further than the premises license.
caseStudies: Stereotype arguments often move from 'all members of group A have trait B' and 'group C is not group A' to 'therefore group C lacks trait B,' which does not follow.
This pattern appears when people treat one pathway to fame, corruption, risk, or success as if it were the only pathway.

Masked man fallacy.definition: Occurs when two names or descriptions refer to the same thing, but a belief or knowledge context blocks simple substitution and the argument ignores that
Masked man fallacy.example: I know who my senator is, but I do not know who wrote this anonymous op-ed, so my senator could not have written it.
Masked man fallacy.notes: In ordinary factual contexts, identical referents can be substituted safely. In belief, knowledge, or perception contexts, that move can fail because the speaker's information is incomplete.
caseStudies: This fallacy shows up whenever people infer identity or non-identity from what someone knows, recognizes, or can name rather than from the underlying facts.
Mystery, anonymity, and pseudonym debates often slide into this mistake by assuming that not knowing a description means the object cannot be the same one known under another description.

Negative proof fallacy.definition: Occurs when a claim is treated as true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved
Negative proof fallacy.example: No one has disproved the hidden vote-switching software, so it is reasonable to believe it exists.
Negative proof fallacy.notes: The rational status of a claim depends on the evidence for it, not on whether someone has managed to close every imaginable contrary possibility.
caseStudies: Election, paranormal, and conspiracy claims often survive by saying 'you cannot prove it did not happen,' as if that absence of disproof supplied positive warrant.
Skeptics can also commit the reverse mistake when they treat an unproved claim as definitively false rather than merely unestablished.

Square logic.definition: Occurs when an argument becomes so internally tangled that its pieces no longer form a coherent chain from premise to conclusion even though it sounds intricate
Square logic.example: If the story were false, fact-checkers would deny it. Because they denied it, they proved it was true, since they only deny dangerous truths.
Square logic.notes: Sometimes the problem is deliberate obscurity; other times it is sincere confusion. Either way, complexity should not be mistaken for structure.
caseStudies: Conspiracy reasoning often spirals into self-sealing loops where every attempted refutation becomes fresh confirmation through an increasingly baroque chain of premises.
AI-generated argument dumps can produce this effect by chaining plausible-sounding clauses that never quite add up to a valid line of reasoning.

Undistributed middle.definition: Occurs when two things are linked to the same broader category and the argument wrongly infers that one of them must therefore be the other
Undistributed middle.example: All conspiracy theorists distrust institutions. I distrust institutions. Therefore I am a conspiracy theorist.
Undistributed middle.notes: Sharing a feature does not establish identity or class inclusion unless the shared feature actually covers the whole relevant group. A middle term can connect without unifying.
caseStudies: Lifestyle and identity marketing often says 'the cool do X' and 'I do X,' then slides to 'therefore I am one of the cool,' even though the shared feature is too broad.
Political commentary frequently infers that because two camps are skeptical of the same institution or support the same policy, they must belong to the same underlying movement.

Circular cause and consequence.definition: Occurs when a feedback loop is treated as if it fully explains, proves, or justifies a result, even though the loop may be contingent, breakable, or not sufficient for the claimed conclusion
Circular cause and consequence.example: The app is not popular because nobody uses it, and nobody uses it because it is not popular, so if people would just use it once it would obviously become a hit.
Circular cause and consequence.notes: Circular dynamics can be real, but identifying a loop does not show that the loop is unstoppable or that breaking one link would guarantee the hoped-for outcome. Further evidence is still needed.
caseStudies: Job markets sometimes create genuine experience loops, but it is still a mistake to assume that every applicant locked out by the loop would necessarily succeed if only one employer made an exception.
Commentators often say a platform is influential because everyone talks about it and everyone talks about it because it is influential, using the loop itself as if it settled the argument.

Conjunction fallacy.definition: Occurs when a more detailed scenario is treated as more probable than a less detailed scenario that already contains it
Conjunction fallacy.example: Because the candidate is young and progressive, it is more likely that she is both a climate activist and a vegan than that she is simply a climate activist.
Conjunction fallacy.notes: Adding conditions never makes a claim more probable than a broader version of that same claim. Extra detail can make a story feel more representative while making it statistically less likely.
caseStudies: Political profiling often mistakes a vivid stereotype for probability, assuming that a person matching one trait is more likely to match an even narrower bundle of traits as well.
AI narratives sometimes suggest that because a model appears articulate, it is more likely to be both highly capable and aligned than merely capable, even though the conjunction is narrower.

Gambler's fallacy.definition: Occurs when someone thinks past outcomes of independent events make a future independent outcome more or less likely than it really is
Gambler's fallacy.example: The coin has landed heads five times in a row, so tails is due next.
Gambler's fallacy.notes: Random sequences naturally contain streaks. When the events are truly independent, the next event does not remember the last one.
caseStudies: People sometimes feel that after many routine flights or medical screenings in a row, a disaster or diagnosis is somehow 'due,' even though independent risks do not balance themselves that way.
In gambling and investing language, talk of a roulette table or slot machine being 'ready to pay out' often confuses a streaky pattern with a real shift in odds.

Prosecutor's fallacy.definition: Occurs when a low probability of a false match is confused with a low probability that a matched person is innocent
Prosecutor's fallacy.example: The facial-recognition system is 99.9% accurate, so the person it flagged must almost certainly be the suspect.
Prosecutor's fallacy.notes: The missing piece is the base rate. Even a very accurate test can generate many false matches when the target condition is rare.
caseStudies: Crime and security debates often overstate the force of DNA, face-recognition, or screening matches by ignoring how many non-matching people were also in the pool.
A similar mistake appears whenever a diagnostic tool's false-positive rate is treated as if it directly gave the chance that any one flagged person is guilty, sick, or dangerous.

Historian's fallacy.definition: Occurs when people in the past are judged as if they had the same information, background assumptions, and hindsight available to later observers
Historian's fallacy.example: Anyone living in 2007 should have seen the financial crash coming exactly as we see it now.
Historian's fallacy.notes: Hindsight compresses uncertainty and highlights the clues that mattered. Real historical agents were working inside a noisier, more limited information environment.
caseStudies: People often imagine they would easily have rejected past medical myths, empires, or moral blind spots, underestimating how strongly institutions and available evidence shape belief.
Post-crisis commentary regularly rewrites messy contingencies into obvious warning signs that were supposedly plain to everyone at the time.

Psychologist's fallacy.definition: Occurs when someone projects their own motives, fears, or mental structure onto others and treats that projection as insight into those other people
Psychologist's fallacy.example: I need religion to keep my impulses in check, so atheists must secretly want religion for the same reason.
Psychologist's fallacy.notes: Self-knowledge can be useful, but it is not a universal template. Other people may share some motives while differing sharply on others.
caseStudies: People often assume that because they would lie, panic, or seek status in a situation, anyone else in that situation must be driven by the same motive.
Political and religious debate is full of claims about what opponents 'really know' or 'really fear' that reflect the speaker's own psychology more than the target's.

Spotlight fallacy.definition: Occurs when the most visible or most covered cases in a category are treated as if they represent the category as a whole
Spotlight fallacy.example: Every protester must be violent because the clips that reached my feed were violent.
Spotlight fallacy.notes: Attention is selective. Media, algorithms, and memory amplify the dramatic cases, not the ordinary distribution.
caseStudies: Crime clips, campus incidents, and viral protest footage often dominate public perception far beyond their representativeness, making whole groups look more extreme than they are.
People watching political interviews can easily conclude that a population is loud, combative, or theatrical without noticing that quieter members of the same population rarely become visible.

Retrospective determinism.definition: Occurs when, after an outcome happens, people claim it was inevitable or obvious all along even though the uncertainty beforehand was real
Retrospective determinism.example: Once the startup collapsed, everyone said its failure had been obvious from day one.
Retrospective determinism.notes: An outcome can make a story feel inevitable in retrospect without ever having been inevitable in advance. Hindsight strips away the branching paths that were live at the time.
caseStudies: After elections, market crashes, and celebrity scandals, commentators often speak as if the final result had been written into the evidence from the start rather than emerging from many uncertain factors.
This fallacy regularly follows close races and volatile technologies, where later narratives overstate how clear the winning path supposedly was.

Intentional fallacy.definition: Occurs when the creator's intended meaning is treated as irrelevant in contexts where that intention is actually important to understanding the work or statement
Intentional fallacy.example: The author says the essay was satirical, but we should ignore that completely and read it only through our own current assumptions.
Intentional fallacy.notes: Authorial intent is not always the only thing that matters, but it is often part of the evidence. Declaring it irrelevant by default can flatten interpretation into projection.
caseStudies: Debates over constitutional language, literature, and political slogans often swing too far toward present-day interpretation while discarding what the author or framers were trying to do.
Online arguments about memes, jokes, and clips frequently ignore context and stated intent altogether, then treat the most inflammatory possible reading as the only serious one.

Equivocation fallacy.definition: Occurs when a broad or harmless sense of a word is used to insinuate a narrower, stronger, or more loaded sense of the same word
Equivocation fallacy.example: The chatbot says it 'understands' the question, so it must understand it in the full human sense.
Equivocation fallacy.notes: The argument trades on the prestige or emotional force of the stronger meaning while relying on the thinner meaning when challenged.
caseStudies: Public arguments about censorship often slide from the general fact that content was moderated to the much stronger charge that it was censored in the same sense as state suppression.
AI marketing repeatedly benefits from equivocation between technical terms such as 'learn,' 'reason,' or 'understand' and their thicker human meanings.

Etymological fallacy.definition: Occurs when a word's original or historical meaning is treated as if it controlled the word's present meaning
Etymological fallacy.example: Because 'literally' once had a narrower sense, any modern emphatic use must be simply wrong.
Etymological fallacy.notes: Words change through use. Present meaning is set by current linguistic convention, not by the oldest recoverable ancestor of the term.
caseStudies: Culture-war and identity debates often turn into fights over what labels 'really mean' based on older usage rather than on how the community currently uses them.
People sometimes defend or condemn a term by appealing to its root language while ignoring the fact that social meaning has moved far beyond the origin.

Bottom-up condemnation.definition: Occurs when a negative generalization about a group is used as if it settled the character or behavior of a specific member of that group
Bottom-up condemnation.example: People in private equity only care about money, so the new board member from that industry is obviously going to gut the program.
Bottom-up condemnation.notes: Even if a group tendency were real, it would not eliminate the need for evidence about the particular person under discussion.
caseStudies: After scandals in policing, finance, or clergy, critics sometimes assume any individual in the profession personally shares the worst traits of the institution.
Online discourse often treats party label, employer, or religious affiliation as if it were enough to prove what a specific person believes or will do.

Bottom-up justification.definition: Occurs when a positive generalization about a group is used as if it established the virtue or competence of a specific member of that group
Bottom-up justification.example: She works for a medical charity, so she must be careful with the facts and impossible to corrupt.
Bottom-up justification.notes: A flattering stereotype is still a stereotype. Group membership can create a first impression, but it does not establish the individual's actual record.
caseStudies: Prestige effects often lead audiences to assume that anyone from a famous university or respected nonprofit is trustworthy even outside their area of expertise.
Voters sometimes infer that a candidate from a reform organization must be personally honest before examining the candidate's own conduct.

Denying the correlative.definition: Occurs when one side of a genuine contrast is denied or redefined so the opposing term has no place to apply
Denying the correlative.example: If the relationship was strong enough to survive it, then it was not really cheating, because real cheating would have ended the relationship.
Denying the correlative.notes: Some concepts only make sense against their correlative opposite. Erasing the contrast does not answer the accusation; it changes the meaning of the term.
caseStudies: Public arguments sometimes say a decision cannot count as censorship unless it was total state control, effectively denying any middle range where the term usefully applies.
Debates about betrayal, fraud, or coercion often narrow the term so drastically that almost no real case can qualify.

For the sake of argument denial.definition: Occurs when a hypothetical premise is rejected simply because the speaker does not actually believe it
For the sake of argument denial.example: You say that even if the policy achieved its stated goal it would still be too costly, but that objection fails because you do not really believe the policy would work.
For the sake of argument denial.notes: Reasoning from an assumption to test its implications is not the same as endorsing the assumption.
caseStudies: Reductio arguments in theology, AI, and politics are often misread as confessions rather than as tests of what would follow if the other side's claim were granted.
Debates stall when a conditional claim such as 'even if you are right, the consequence would still be unacceptable' is treated as if it were a statement of belief.

Homunculus fallacy.definition: Occurs when a mind-like inner observer is smuggled in to explain mind-like abilities, thereby postponing rather than solving the explanation
Homunculus fallacy.example: Vision works because the brain forms an internal picture and then an inner observer looks at that picture.
Homunculus fallacy.notes: If the inner observer can already do the job, the original explanatory problem just reappears one level down.
caseStudies: Popular neuroscience writing sometimes says that the brain 'decides' or a memory center 'knows' in ways that merely rename the puzzle rather than explain it.
Criticism of AI can do something similar when it assumes a hidden module inside the system literally understands the output in the same way a person would.

Human standard fallacy.definition: Occurs when a human classification, rule, or label is treated as if it automatically determined the underlying fact or moral status
Human standard fallacy.example: The platform's policy now defines this claim as misinformation, so it became false the moment the label was applied.
Human standard fallacy.notes: Institutional labels can matter legally or practically, but they do not by themselves create truth, value, or natural kinds.
caseStudies: Markets and media often confuse approved, certified, or official with true, safe, or just.
Political rhetoric often treats whatever a legislature recognizes or forbids as automatically morally right or wrong.

Impotent logical space.definition: Occurs when a view is framed so every possible outcome fits it equally well, leaving no meaningful room for the claim to fail
Impotent logical space.example: If the forecast comes true, the psychic was right; if it fails, the warning changed the future, which also proves the psychic was right.
Impotent logical space.notes: A claim that survives every observation unchanged may be emotionally resilient, but it has surrendered explanatory power.
caseStudies: Conspiracy systems often explain both the presence and the absence of evidence as confirmation.
Some technology hype frames both success and failure as proof that general intelligence is just around the corner.

Inconsistent comparison.definition: Occurs when different comparison targets are used across different dimensions to create the illusion of one all-around winner
Inconsistent comparison.example: This laptop is cheaper than Brand A, lighter than Brand B, and faster than Brand C, so it is plainly the best laptop on the market.
Inconsistent comparison.notes: A complete comparison needs a consistent baseline or a transparent weighting of tradeoffs, not a collage of unrelated best cases.
caseStudies: Consumer ads often compare each feature against whichever rival looks weakest on that feature, then announce overall superiority.
Campaign brag sheets sometimes do the same by mixing job growth, crime, housing, and graduation metrics against different jurisdictions and different years.

Is-ought problem.definition: Occurs when a descriptive claim about what is common, natural, or actual is treated as if it directly established what ought to be done
Is-ought problem.example: Most companies monitor workers in some form now, so employees ought to accept constant tracking as normal.
Is-ought problem.notes: An ought needs a normative premise about goals, duties, or values. Facts alone do not generate that extra step.
caseStudies: Arguments about gender, family, and competition often slide from claims about what is common in nature to claims about what is therefore morally required.
Workplace norms are regularly defended by saying they are simply how the market works, even when the moral question is precisely whether the market should work that way.

Linearity fallacy.definition: Occurs when someone assumes that doubling the input will double the output even though the system has thresholds, saturation, feedback loops, or diminishing returns
Linearity fallacy.example: One dose gave a modest result, so taking twice as much should produce twice the benefit.
Linearity fallacy.notes: Many real systems change slowly at first, then rapidly, then plateau, or even reverse after a threshold.
caseStudies: Growth forecasts for social platforms often assume audience reach will keep scaling smoothly even after attention markets saturate.
Policy debates about climate, housing, and healthcare frequently ignore the non-linear effects of bottlenecks, incentives, and behavioral feedback.

Overwhelming exception.definition: Occurs when a general principle is padded with so many exceptions that it no longer guides action or says much of substance
Overwhelming exception.example: I believe in free expression, except when the speech is offensive, politically costly, factually shaky, socially awkward, or risky to my side.
Overwhelming exception.notes: A principle can have limits, but if the exceptions swallow the rule, the apparent commitment becomes mostly decorative.
caseStudies: Public commitments to transparency, merit, or local control often vanish once they threaten a favored outcome.
Organizations sometimes advertise simple values statements that become practically meaningless once the long list of carve-outs is revealed.

Pathetic fallacy.definition: Occurs when human feelings, intentions, or judgments are projected onto impersonal things and then treated as if the projection explained reality
Pathetic fallacy.example: The market is punishing voters today because it is afraid of reform.
Pathetic fallacy.notes: Personifying weather, markets, or algorithms can be a vivid metaphor, but it becomes fallacious when the metaphor is used as literal evidence.
caseStudies: People often say the algorithm hates them, loves outrage, or wants to silence them when the actual explanation is a mix of optimization rules and incentives.
News coverage sometimes treats storms, markets, or viruses as if they were moral agents taking revenge, sending messages, or rewarding virtue.

Perverted analogy.definition: Occurs when an analogy is deliberately stretched past its intended point so it can be mocked or refuted
Perverted analogy.example: Calling public-health reserves an insurance policy is silly, because insurance companies do not hire epidemiologists.
Perverted analogy.notes: An analogy usually highlights one structural similarity, not a one-to-one mapping of every detail.
caseStudies: Infrastructure analogies about bridges, firewalls, or guardrails are often attacked by demanding that every literal feature transfer over exactly.
Debaters sometimes turn an opponent's limited comparison into a cartoon version so they can say the analogy obviously fails.

Regression fallacy.definition: Occurs when movement back toward a normal range after an extreme result is credited to some intervention that may have had little or nothing to do with it
Regression fallacy.example: The student had an unusually bad test, got lectured by the teacher, and then scored closer to normal on the next test, so the lecture must have caused the improvement.
Regression fallacy.notes: After unusually high or low outcomes, partial reversion toward the average is often expected even without special causal forces.
caseStudies: Sports commentators routinely over-credit halftime speeches or rituals for rebounds that would be unsurprising after an extreme first-half performance.
Investors and managers often mistake a natural bounce after a terrible quarter for proof that a new slogan, consultant, or memo fixed the underlying problem.

Semantic pixelization.definition: Occurs when a fuzzy, graded, or probabilistic position is forced into unnaturally sharp categories so it becomes easier to attack
Semantic pixelization.example: If you say the rollout is probably safe, are you claiming it is perfectly safe with zero chance of failure?
Semantic pixelization.notes: Many concepts such as belief, risk, identity, and influence work by degree. Treating them as all-or-nothing can falsify the speaker's actual position.
caseStudies: Election, public-health, and AI debates often force nuanced confidence claims into binary boxes such as certain or uncertain, safe or unsafe, real or fake.
Arguments about what someone believes frequently replace a spectrum of confidence with a yes-or-no label that the original speaker never endorsed.

Suppressed correlative.definition: Occurs when one term in a meaningful contrast is redefined so broadly or so narrowly that its opposing term can no longer do any work
Suppressed correlative.example: No one is really healthy, because there is always someone healthier.
Suppressed correlative.notes: Correlative terms such as healthy and unhealthy, free and restricted, informed and uninformed, or biased and impartial depend on contrasts that can be weakened without disappearing.
caseStudies: Critics sometimes argue that because everyone has some bias, calling a report biased says nothing, as if degrees of distortion and unfairness were impossible.
Debates about freedom and censorship often set the positive term to an impossible ideal so that ordinary, useful distinctions collapse.

Suppressed correlative (DUPLICATE).definition: Occurs when a contrast term is emptied by redefining its counterpart so the distinction collapses
Suppressed correlative (DUPLICATE).example: Everyone has some bias, so calling this report biased tells us nothing.
Suppressed correlative (DUPLICATE).notes: The fact that a property comes in degrees does not erase the usefulness of the distinction. This duplicate record is kept in sync so both site entries carry a modernized explanation.
caseStudies: Public arguments often pretend that if no one is perfectly objective, then objectivity and bias can never be discussed in meaningful comparative terms.
A similar move appears when people say every restriction limits freedom somehow, therefore no restriction can be singled out as unusually coercive.

Top-down condemnation.definition: Occurs when a negative trait found in one member of a group is used to condemn the group as a whole
Top-down condemnation.example: One rideshare driver ran a scam on me, so rideshare drivers are crooks.
Top-down condemnation.notes: A vivid case can motivate investigation, but it does not by itself justify a population-level conclusion.
caseStudies: Isolated crime stories are often turned into sweeping claims about immigrants, professions, age groups, or political movements.
A single corporate scandal can quickly become a claim that the entire industry is rotten in exactly the same way.

Top-down faulty generalization.definition: Occurs when a reasonable generalization is attacked by demanding that it hold without relevant scope conditions or exceptions
Top-down faulty generalization.example: You say processed sugar is unhealthy, but endurance athletes use sugar during races, so your generalization collapses.
Top-down faulty generalization.notes: Generalizations are often default-pattern claims, not exceptionless universal laws.
caseStudies: Public-health advice is often dismissed by pointing to unusual edge cases even when the advice was clearly aimed at ordinary conditions.
Safety rules and economic patterns are frequently challenged by exceptions that do not actually undermine the broader tendency being described.

Top-down justification.definition: Occurs when a positive trait found in one member of a group is used to justify a positive conclusion about the group as a whole
Top-down justification.example: My landlord fixed things promptly, so landlords get an unfairly bad reputation.
Top-down justification.notes: A favorable anecdote can remind us not to overgeneralize negatively, but it cannot prove that the larger class is generally positive.
caseStudies: One transparent politician or one ethical corporation is often used to imply that the surrounding system is healthier than the broader evidence suggests.
People frequently infer that an institution is trustworthy because they personally encountered one helpful employee inside it.
